title: Auth and Authorization in MCP
description: Secure MCP servers with authentication, authorization, scoped access, and safe credential management in C#.

blocks.text: MCP servers often expose sensitive business logic or data. Use authentication to identify clients, authorization to enforce permissions, and scoped access to limit what each client can call or read.

blocks.title: Recommended security controls
items: **Transport security** - use TLS for HTTP transports.
**Client authentication** - API keys, OAuth, or mTLS depending on deployment.
**Tool authorization** - restrict which clients can invoke sensitive tools.
**Resource scoping** - limit resources by tenant, user, or environment.
**Audit logging** - record who called what, when, and with which arguments.

blocks.title: Conceptual authorization filter
blocks.content: Simplified authorization check for tool invocation.

blocks.title: Never trust the client
blocks.text: Validate the caller identity on every request. Do not rely on arguments submitted by the client to enforce access control.

items.text: All MCP traffic uses TLS in production
items.hint: HTTP transports must not run over plain HTTP with sensitive data

items.text: I authenticate every request before executing tools or returning resources
items.hint: Do not trust headers or arguments submitted by the client

items.text: I audit sensitive tool calls and resource reads
items.hint: Log caller identity, operation, timestamp, and outcome

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: MCP servers need the same security rigor as REST APIs.
Authenticate callers, authorize actions, and scope resource access.
Audit logs help detect misuse and debug failures.
blocks.takeaway: If a tool can change data or expose private information, it must be protected by authentication and authorization.
